Verdicts depend on matching words in error text.

terms.meaning: a real but very small request sent to a service to confirm it works now
the label given to a check result, such as ok or gateway-auth

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and purpose
sections.what: Loads the model call, key status, and role settings. The header explains the three failures this check exists to tell apart.
sections.watch_out: Renaming any imported function breaks this check.

sections.name: LiveCheckVerdict
sections.title: Possible outcome labels
sections.what: Lists every label a check can return: ok, not configured, gateway auth, provider key, model not found, rate limited, usage limit, timeout, and unknown.
sections.why: Likely reason: fixed labels that health screens and tests can compare.
sections.watch_out: A new label needs matching advice in the classifier.

sections.name: LiveCheckResult
sections.title: Shape of one check result
sections.what: Defines the fields of one check result, including the role checked, the model, latency, scrubbed error, advice, and key status names.
sections.why: Likely reason: one consistent report for health output.
sections.watch_out: Key status shows names only, by design. Values must never be added here.

sections.name: scrubKeyMaterial
sections.title: Removing key text from errors
sections.what: Removes anything that looks like a key or bearer token from error text, replacing it with a redaction marker.
sections.why: The header states that the upstream echoes partly masked keys, which still leak their start and end.
sections.watch_out: Only known key shapes are caught. A key in a new format could still leak.

sections.name: classifyLiveError
sections.title: Turning an error into a verdict
sections.what: Reads the error text and any status code in it, and returns a verdict with a short piece of advice.
sections.why: The header and the branch comments explain each category, especially that a model scoping error looks like an auth error.
sections.watch_out: The rule that matches integration and key is broad and could match unrelated messages.

sections.name: runModelLiveCheck
sections.title: Running one live check
sections.what: Sends one five-token call to the chosen model and returns success with latency, or the classified and scrubbed failure.
sections.why: The header describes a cheap call through the real transport.
sections.watch_out: Retries are off on purpose, so a single transient error is reported as a failure.

sections.name: runRoleLiveChecks
sections.title: Running one check per role
sections.what: Runs the live check once for each role in turn.
sections.why: The comment states this proves the role wiring, not only the model name.
sections.watch_out: Checks run one after another, so total time grows with each role added.

summary: Makes one tiny real model call per role and reports why it failed, if it did, with secret text removed.
purpose: Tell apart a rejected gateway login, a bad upstream provider key, a wrong model name, a rate limit, a spent usage limit, and a timeout.
why: The header states these failures look the same from outside. Error text is scrubbed because the upstream provider echoes partly masked keys.
how: Picks the role's model, confirms that a transport exists, sends a five-token ping with retries off, classifies any error text into a verdict, removes key-like text, and returns the result with key status names.
inputs: A timeout, an optional role, and the environment settings read by the transport and model modules.
outputs: A result object with ok, verdict, model, base address, latency, scrubbed error text, advice, and key status names.
risks: Classification matches words in error text, so new wording falls to unknown. Each check spends a small amount of real money. The scrubbing only catches key shapes it knows.
debug: Read rawError and verdict first. If verdict is unknown, read the raw text as written. If verdict is not-configured, check the secrets for the Portkey and OpenAI keys. Compare the model in the result with the role settings in modelConfig.
